options: The job definition row in msdb.dbo.sysjobs, with no steps and no server target yet
A fully runnable job, including its schedule
A new SQL Server Agent Windows service
A linked server entry
questions.explain: sp_add_job only creates the sysjobs row. Steps come from sp_add_jobstep, and the job isn't runnable until sp_add_jobserver targets it at a server.

questions.q: Which subsystem would a job step use to run a PowerShell script?
options: PowerShell
TSQL
CmdExec only, since PowerShell isn't a real subsystem
SSIS
questions.explain: sp_add_jobstep's @subsystem parameter accepts PowerShell directly as one of its execution engines, alongside TSQL, CmdExec, and SSIS.

questions.q: A job has steps but never appears scheduled to run anywhere. What call is missing?
options: sp_add_jobserver, which targets the job at a server so it can actually execute
sp_add_job, which must be called twice
sp_add_operator
sp_add_alert
questions.explain: Even a job with steps needs sp_add_jobserver to attach it to a server; on a standalone instance that's always (local).

options: Whether the job moves to the next step, quits reporting success, or quits reporting failure when that step fails
Which operator gets emailed
The schedule the job runs on
Whether the step retries an unlimited number of times automatically
questions.explain: on_success_action and on_fail_action define per-step branching behavior between steps in a multi-step job.

questions.q: Which subsystem would you use for a step that runs an operating-system command like robocopy?
options: CmdExec
TSQL
SSIS
PowerShell is required for all OS-level commands
questions.explain: CmdExec runs an operating-system command or executable directly; robocopy is a classic CmdExec step example.
